title: Design rider assignment for food delivery
dek: At 8:30 pm Zotato has 3 lakh riders on the road and hundreds of new orders every second. Pick the right rider for each order, so the food is picked up just as it's ready, and never give one rider two orders by mistake.

items: Riders' phones send their location every few seconds. Keep only the latest location per rider, in memory, in a map split into small cells per city. Don't write every ping to a database.

For a new order, look up free riders in the cells around the restaurant, and score them by how soon they can get there compared with when the food will be ready. The nearest rider isn't always the best one.
Offer the order to one rider at a time, holding them for 20 seconds. The hold is a conditional change (only if still free), so two orders can never grab the same rider.
At the peak, decide every few seconds for all waiting orders together, rather than one at a time; it gives better pairs overall.
A location older than about 30 seconds means the rider is out of signal or offline; leave them out.
Track every active rider's location and status (free, offered, assigned, delivering).
For each new order, choose a rider and offer it; if they decline or don't answer, offer it to the next.
Aim for the rider to reach the restaurant around when the food is ready: not early (waiting), not late (cold food).
Out of scope here: routing and maps, rider pay, and live tracking for customers (which reads the same locations).

body.label: Qualities to aim for
head: Quality
Target
rows: A first offer within a few seconds of the order being accepted by the restaurant
A rider is never offered two orders at once
Locations are usually a few seconds old; riders silent for 30 seconds are left out
3 lakh riders online at dinner, about 350 orders a second at the peak

items: Location pings: 3 lakh riders × one every 4 seconds is 75,000 updates a second at dinner.
Latest locations: 3 lakh × about 100 bytes is 30 MB. It all fits in memory several times over; the problem is the update rate, not the size.
Orders: 1 crore a day, with about a quarter between 8 and 10 pm, is about 350 orders a second at the peak.
Each order looks at maybe 30 to 50 nearby free riders. 350 × 50 is under 20,000 rider checks a second: small for an in-memory map.
History: 75,000 pings × 100 bytes is 7.5 MB a second, about 27 GB an hour, kept in cheap storage for travel-time estimates and disputes.
Rider: `id`, `city`, `status`, `lat`, `lng`, `updated_at`, `offer_order_id`, `offer_until`.
Order: `id`, `restaurant`, `ready_at` (the kitchen's estimate), `status`, `rider_id`, `offers_tried`.
Cell: a small hexagon or square of the city, holding the ids of free riders inside it, kept in memory.

body.label: API
body.say: Riders send their location every few seconds. Offers are pushed to the rider app. Accepting succeeds only while the offer still stands.

body.cap: Rider apps send locations to a location service that keeps only the latest one per rider, in an in-memory map of the city. For a new order, the dispatcher asks the map for free riders near the restaurant, scores them, and offers the order to the best.

body.x: Split everything by city: Pune's riders never take Chennai's orders, so each city's map and dispatcher can live on their own machines, and a problem in one city stays in that city. Draw cities as service zones (Gurugram apart from Delhi), and give each rider to one zone at a time.

body.name: First try
body.kind: A DATABASE ROW PER RIDER, UPDATED ON EVERY PING
body.what: UPDATE riders SET lat, lng on every ping, and query "free riders within 2 km" with a geo index for each order.
body.use: Simple, and fine for a few thousand riders.
body.avoid: 75,000 updates a second to rows that a geo index must reshuffle each time, with the dispatcher reading the same rows. The database spends dinner time moving dots around.
body.ex: At 8:30 pm the riders table falls behind, and the dispatcher offers orders to riders who moved 2 km since.
body.like: Writing every rider's position on a whiteboard by hand, every 4 seconds.

body.name: Better
body.kind: LATEST LOCATION IN MEMORY, BY CELL
body.what: A location service per city keeps each rider's latest ping in memory and in the right cell of a grid (geohash or hexagons). Free riders near a point are the riders in its cell and the cells around it. Every ping also goes to a log for history.
body.use: Updates are a memory write; nearby lookups read a few cells. One machine handles a big city.
body.avoid: Memory is lost on a crash. Locations come back with the next pings, within seconds, and a standby copy reads the log. Rider status (free, offered, assigned) can't come back from pings, so it lives in a small durable store.
body.ex: An order at Koregaon Park reads 7 cells and finds 42 free riders in under a millisecond.
body.like: Riders standing in numbered squares on a map; to find someone near a spot, you look at that square and its neighbours.

items: Nearest isn't best. A rider 3 minutes away for food ready in 15 minutes waits 12 minutes at the restaurant, while a rider 12 minutes away arrives just in time.
Score each candidate: travel time to the restaurant (from road distances, not straight lines) against the food's ready time, plus things like their current direction and how long they've been idle.

At the busiest times, collect the orders and free riders of the last few seconds and pair them all at once. One order's best rider might be the only good rider for another order; deciding together avoids that clash.

body.x: One order at a time per rider

body.cap: A rider goes free → offered (held for 20 seconds) → assigned → delivering → free. A decline or no answer in 20 seconds puts them back to free, and the order goes to the next rider.

items: Making the offer is a conditional change in that status store, the one place every dispatcher checks: set status to offered only if it's still free. Status changes a few times per order, so this store stays quiet next to the pings. If two dispatchers try at once, one wins and the other picks someone else.
The offer expires after 20 seconds. Accepting after that gets a polite "already gone"; the order has moved on.
Accepting is also conditional: only if the offer is still this rider's. A rider tapping twice changes nothing.
A rider's pings stop (a tunnel, a dead phone): after about 30 seconds they're left out of new offers, but keep any order they already have.
A city's location service dies: the standby takes over; within a few seconds every rider has pinged again and the map is whole. Who is offered or assigned is safe in the status store.
No rider accepts after several tries: widen the search area, tell the restaurant, and update the customer's delivery time honestly.
Junior / mid: riders sending locations, finding nearby free riders, offering an order and handling a decline.
Senior: in-memory cells instead of database writes per ping, the ping numbers, scoring by ready time, the 20-second hold as a conditional change.
Lead: splitting by city, batch matching at the peak, standby and rebuild from pings, stale riders, and what the customer is told.
"Give one rider two orders from the same restaurant?" Batch them when both are ready within a few minutes and the drops are close; score the pair as one trip.
"Live tracking for customers?" Read the rider's latest location from the same map, a few times a minute; never from the database.
"Rain, and half the riders go offline?" Fewer candidates per order: widen the area, slow new orders with honest delivery times, and ask more riders to come online.
"Faking location?" Check that pings move at believable speeds and match the route; flag riders who jump.
"How do you test it?" Replay a recorded dinner of pings and orders against the dispatcher and compare waiting times at restaurants and doors.

body.x: Dispatch has a dinner rush every day. The lunch and dinner rush challenge practises sizing for two daily peaks.
body.go: Try the lunch and dinner rush challenge

practice.brief: Each test sends rider location pings and order offers. Each updates or reads the in-memory map of riders: 1 query, which a cache (memory) answers 95% of the time. Your Clients' own rate is ignored.

tests.name: A normal afternoon
tests.desc: 25,000 location pings and offers a second in the afternoon.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of pings and offers succeed
Riders' latest positions are held where "nearest to this point" is quick to answer
Orders are matched to riders by workers, away from the location pings

tests.name: Dinner
tests.desc: 75,000 a second for an hour from 8 pm: 3 lakh riders pinging every 4 seconds.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of pings and offers succeed

tests.name: Rain at 8 pm
tests.desc: It starts raining in Mumbai: everyone orders in and riders ping more often: 1.1 lakh a second for 15 minutes from 8 pm.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of pings and offers succeed
Location pings are queued for the workers

tests.name: A server group dies
tests.desc: At the peak (75,000 a second) the busiest group of servers crashes; it is back 5 minutes later.

checks.label: At least 99.5% of pings and offers still succeed
No server group that every request depends on (no single point of failure)

tests.name: The database fails
tests.desc: At the peak the busiest database crashes. With a standby in another zone it fails over in 2 minutes; without one it is down for 30.

checks.label: At least 99.8% of pings and offers still succeed
Every database has a standby in another zone (Multi-AZ)

tests.name: A sensible bill
tests.desc: A whole day at the normal rate (25,000 a second). Paying for far more than the traffic needs fails, like a memory limit.

checks.label: At least 99.9% of pings and offers succeed

tests.name: A rider moves
tests.desc: Rider r1 sends a new position from the rider app. Only the latest position is kept; the trail goes to cheap storage later.

tests.name: An order needs a rider
tests.desc: The restaurant accepts order #91. It is recorded as waiting for a rider; choosing one and sending the offer follows a moment later.

fr.label: Track each rider's location and status
Choose a rider for a new order and offer it
If declined or no answer, offer the next rider
Arrive when the food is ready
Never offer a rider two orders at once

est.label: Location pings a second at dinner
Orders a second at peak
est.how: a quarter of 1 crore in 2 hours

decisions.q: Riders send their location every 4 seconds. Where does it go?
options: A new row in the main database for every single ping that arrives
An in-memory geo index with only the latest position
Kept on the rider's phone until an order needs it
decisions.why: 75,000 pings a second would bury the main database, and asking phones on demand is slow. Matching only needs where each rider is now; the trail goes to cheap storage for later.

decisions.q: How do you choose a rider for a new order?
options: Offer it to every free rider nearby; the first to accept wins
Give it to the free rider who has waited longest in the city
Look at the nearest few free riders and offer to one at a time
decisions.why: A few nearby candidates keep the search small, and one offer at a time, with a timeout, avoids several riders racing for the same order. The longest-waiting rider may be across the city.

decisions.q: A rider must never get two orders at once. How?
options: Mark the rider as offered in one atomic step
Check the rider is free, then assign the order
Let the rider app decline an order if they're busy
decisions.why: Between a separate check and assign, a second order can claim the same rider. An atomic "offer only if free" means exactly one order can claim each rider; relying on the app to decline still sends two offers.

hints.x: Riders, orders and offers. Which rule protects a rider from two orders at once?
Pings dominate: riders ÷ seconds between pings. The data itself is tiny.
POST a location from the rider app; offers are pushed to the rider; POST accept (409 if it expired).
75,000 pings a second must never touch a disk one by one. Keep the latest locations in memory (a Cache).
Queue the pings; workers update the map by cell; history goes to cheap storage later.
Rain makes everything busier at once: size for it before 8 pm, and keep two groups everywhere.

wrong.name: No cache
wrong.why: Every read goes to the database, which can't take the peak.

wrong.name: One server group
wrong.why: When it crashes, nothing answers for 5 minutes.

wrong.name: Single-zone database
wrong.why: A crash keeps it down for 30 minutes.

wrong.name: No queue
wrong.why: The burst hits the database directly and crashes it.

wrong.name: Biggest everything
wrong.why: Passes the load but costs far more than the traffic needs.

wrong.name: Right sizes, general parts
wrong.why: The sizes and redundancy are right, but no component does the job this problem turns on, so the design would carry the traffic without doing what was asked.

wrong.name: Riders without a position
wrong.why: The riders table has no position, so a location ping has nowhere to go and no one can find the nearest free rider.
